extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of mathematics history; general math enthusiasts
extracted.subtask_short: historical account of failed FLT proofs
extracted.subtask_description: A short historical narrative describing Gabriel Lamé's and Augustin-Louis Cauchy's attempted proofs of Fermat's Last Theorem, the logical gap discovered by Kummer, and the role of unique factorisation. Intended as a pedagogical/history-of-math entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique factorisation requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs based on unique factorisation must ensure the property holds in the domain being used: that every integer (or element) can be broken down into a single series of prime factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: "Kummer... had become aware that the two mathematicians had based their proof on a property known as unique factorisation. This stated in substance that every integer number could be broken down into a single series of prime numbers... in the field of complex numbers, this property is not necessarily true. The lack of unique factorisation could have been worked round with some techniques but however there remained some recalcitrant numbers." Ensure the ring or field you work in actually has unique factorisation before using it in a proof; otherwise supply alternative techniques or address exceptional elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish complete proofs for verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of a proof should be accompanied by the complete proof, not merely statements or extracts, so others can verify correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: "These mathematicians set the Parisian salons on fire with statements and extracts of their respective proofs but without ever publishing the complete proofs." In practice, partial announcements prevent proper peer checking and can mask errors; full publication is required for scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a general solution, not only case-by-case fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: When problematic cases are infinite in number, handling individual instances does not constitute a general proof; the argument must address all (infinitely many) cases or show a general mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: "These numbers could in theory have been faced singly, but being infinite that would not have resolved the problem." A valid proof should avoid reducing correctness to infinitely many ad-hoc verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for logical errors; do not rely on unchecked assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the logical steps of a proof carefully; hidden or unchecked assumptions can render an argument fallacious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page: "Kummer... had become aware that the proofs followed the same reasoning and that they contained a logical error that rendered them fallacious." Explicitly identify and justify all assumptions (e.g., properties of the number system used) to prevent subtle logical mistakes.
